angle.text: Personality maxxing works through impressions: people who are engaging, relaxed and have things to talk about are described by practitioners as being seen as more attractive, and members who already work on their appearance use it to round out the overall impression.

lead: Personality maxxing is the looksmaxxing-community term for improving the non-physical side of attractiveness: social skills, humor, confidence, hobbies, interests and general presence. Practitioners treat it as a complement to facial and body work, on the view that how a person comes across in conversation, and what they do with their life, changes how attractive they are seen to be, especially once a first impression has passed.[1]

Typical activities discussed under the label include building skills and hobbies, becoming more socially fluent, improving conversation and humor, developing a personal style and cultivating interests that make a person more engaging to others. It is a lifestyle approach rather than a product or procedure, and no formal research programme exists under this name.

Social psychology does describe factors beyond physical looks that influence attraction. Wikipedia's article on interpersonal attraction reports that displaying traits such as kindness is associated with being rated more attractive, that shared attitudes and especially shared activities and interests predict liking, and that familiarity tends to increase it.[2] The halo effect literature adds that impressions run both ways: attractive people are often credited with desirable traits, and beauty filters have been found to raise ratings of sociability and happiness.[3]
infobox: Social skills, style, confidence, moneymaxxing, fitness

paras: The term follows the community habit of adding the suffix -maxxing to any area people try to optimise. Here the area is personality and interests rather than face or body. On looksmax.org it is often mentioned next to moneymaxxing as one of the non-facial levers of success.[1]

One looksmax.org member argues that looks matter mostly for the first impression, while keeping a relationship or friendship requires a decent personality, and that people with good faces but off-putting personalities do not retain others' interest beyond early dates.[1]

Other members take the opposite position, as in a thread titled around hobbies, interests and backgrounds meaning nothing, and some describe feeling that a lack of talent or interests is a disadvantage.[4][5] A further thread jokes that interest in the looksmaxxing project itself had crowded out earlier hobbies.[6]

Wikipedia's overview of interpersonal attraction reports that similarity in attitudes and values correlates with attraction, that shared activities and interests were especially predictive of liking, that perceived similarity can predict initial attraction better than actual similarity, and that repeated exposure usually increases liking.[2]

The same article cites a 2014 study in which people displaying kindness were seen as more attractive.[2] Research on the halo effect, beginning with Thorndike in 1920 and the 1972 Dion, Berscheid and Walster study, shows that physical attractiveness shapes assumptions about personality, and that the reverse can also occur, with attractive people sometimes judged as more conceited.[3]

Within the community, personality work is usually presented as a companion to physical improvement and as something available to everyone at little cost, though members disagree about how much it adds compared with facial structure.[1][4]
